lines.show: Most cancer drugs fail before they reach a patient.
For decades, cancer cells have been grown flat, in a plastic dish.
So labs now grow something closer to the real thing: tiny 3D copies of a patient's tumour, called organoids.
This year, two leading cancer centres used organoids to switch off every gene, one at a time, and find the ones a cancer can't live without.
Hundreds of genes mattered more in organoids than in flat cells, and those are now being put forward as drug targets.
Here's the catch.
Organoids change two things at once.
One is the shape. 3D instead of flat.
The other is the food.
Cells in a dish live in a liquid called the medium.
Organoids get a clean, lab-made medium with almost no cholesterol.
So when a gene matters more in an organoid, which change caused it?
The data to tell them apart already existed.
A big public database had flat cells grown on the organoid medium.
Same diet, no 3D shape.
If a gene matters more there too, the shape can't explain it. The food can.
With Muse, Meta's AI model, running the research loop, we checked all 17,525 genes.
456 clearly behave differently in organoids.
So how many of those 456 also change when the only thing you change is the food?
Eighty-five percent.
So the effect may not come from the tumour's 3D shape at all. It may come from what we feed it.
And in a patient, a tumour is fed by blood, which is full of cholesterol.
So a weakness that only shows up on a diet with almost no cholesterol may not exist in the patient at all.
But there's a simple way to check.
Put the cholesterol back into the organoid's food.
If these genes stop mattering, it was the food. If they still matter, they're stronger candidates.
All of this is free at itsthemedium.com.
Researchers can paste their own list of genes and see in seconds which ones look like diet effects.
For the follow-up test, Meta's SAM 3.1 outlines and measures every organoid in a lab's own microscope images.
And Muse answers questions by searching the full table with its own tools, showing every step.
Organoids are still a big step forward.
We just need to check what we're feeding them.
It's the Medium.
